**Rationale**

Ki-67, encoded by **MKI67**, is one of the most established single-cell markers of active proliferation. It is very low or absent in quiescent G0 cells and increases as cells enter and progress through G1, S, G2, and M phases. In breast cancer, Ki-67 protein is clinically used as a proliferation index, and at the single-cell level its abundance is expected to reflect the fraction of tumor cells actively traversing the cell cycle. Because the analysis described computationally excludes infiltrating blood cells, the remaining Ki-67 variation among tumor-enriched cells is most parsimoniously explained by tumor-intrinsic heterogeneity in cell-cycle state rather than by contamination from proliferating immune cells.

The core molecular switch controlling cell-cycle entry is the **cyclin D–CDK4/6–cyclin E–CDK2–RB1–E2F** axis. Mitogenic signaling induces **CCND1** and CDK4/6 activity, followed by **CCNE1/CDK2** activation. These kinases phosphorylate **RB1**, relieving RB/DREAM-mediated repression of E2F target genes. E2F activation drives the S-phase and proliferation gene program, and Ki-67 protein accumulates in cells that have entered this active cell-cycle state. Conversely, cells with hypophosphorylated RB1, high CDK inhibitor activity such as **CDKN1B/p27**, and low E2F activity are expected to remain Ki-67-low.

**Specific hypothesis**

I hypothesize that **cell-to-cell variation in Ki-67 protein abundance among breast cancer cells is primarily driven by heterogeneous activation of the CCND1/CDK4/6–CCNE1/CDK2–RB1 phosphorylation–E2F1/2 transcriptional axis, corresponding to variable G1/S cell-cycle entry and progression**. Under this model, Ki-67-high tumor cells are those with high phospho-RB1, high E2F target gene expression, and S/G2/M cell-cycle identity, whereas Ki-67-low tumor cells are in a hypophosphorylated-RB1, E2F-repressed G0/G1-like state.

This conclusion is best classified as **(a) established literature knowledge**, formulated here as a specific, testable single-cell spatial hypothesis. Supporting literature includes the original characterization of Ki-67 as a proliferation-associated nuclear antigen and reviews of its biology (Gerdes et al., *Int J Cancer*, 1983; Scholzen & Gerdes, *J Cell Physiol*, 2000), the canonical RB/E2F cell-cycle control pathway (Dyson, *Genes Dev*, 1998), the role of RB/DREAM complexes in cell-cycle gene repression (Sadasivam & DeCaprio, *Nat Rev Cancer*, 2013), and the dependence of CDK4/6 inhibitor response on RB-intact cell-cycle control in breast cancer (Dean et al., *Oncogene*, 2010).

**Experimentally testable prediction**

In the CosMx data, Ki-67 protein abundance should correlate strongly with independent cell-cycle and E2F-activity markers, such as **CCNE1, PCNA, MCM genes, TOP2A, CCNB1, CDK1, FOXM1**, and an E2F target score that excludes MKI67/Ki-67 to avoid circularity. On orthogonal tissue sections, multiplex immunofluorescence should show that Ki-67-high tumor cells co-express **phospho-RB1** and S/G2/M markers, while Ki-67-low tumor cells show higher **CDKN1B/p27** and hypophosphorylated RB1. Functionally, in RB1-competent breast cancer cell lines or patient-derived organoids, pharmacologic inhibition of **CDK4/6** with palbociclib or inhibition of **CDK2** should reduce RB1 phosphorylation, suppress E2F target expression, and decrease Ki-67 protein abundance. Conversely, cells with RB1 loss or constitutive E2F activation should show less CDK4/6 inhibitor-sensitive Ki-67 reduction.
